question.text:
\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} q_{11} & q_{12} \\ q_{21} & q_{22} \\ q_{31} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{q_{32}} \\ \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{12}} \\ 0 & r_{22} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $q_{32} \cdot r_{12}.$
question.explanation:
Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

Step 1. We set $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

Step 2. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

\begin{align} \mathbf{v}_2 &= \mathbf{a}_2- \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{a}_2 \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a}_2-\dfrac{\mathbf{a}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{6}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{q}_1 & = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{q}_2 & =\dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align}

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} R &= Q^TA \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & 2\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{2\sqrt{3}} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Finally, $q_{32} \cdot r_{12} = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\right) \cdot \left(2\sqrt{3}\right) = \sqrt{2}.$

example.title: Finding the QR Factorization of a Matrix

question.text:
\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \mathbf{q}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{11}} & r_{12} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{13}} \\ 0 & r_{22} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{23}} \\ 0 & 0 & r_{33} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R} \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{q}_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{a}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_2 = \dfrac{1}{5}\mathbf{a}_2 + 6\mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_3 = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{a}_3 - 2\mathbf{q}_1 + \mathbf{q}_2 \end{cases} \]

What is the value of $r_{11}+r_{13}+r_{23}?$
question.explanation:
Let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$ \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{q}_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{a}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_2 = \dfrac{1}{5}\mathbf{a}_2 + 6\mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_3 = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{a}_3 - 2\mathbf{q}_1 + \mathbf{q}_2 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} \mathbf{a}_1 = 3\mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{a}_2 = -30\mathbf{q}_1 + 5\mathbf{q}_2 \\ \mathbf{a}_3 = 8\mathbf{q}_1 - 4\mathbf{q}_2 + 4\mathbf{q}_3. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, this system can be written in matrix form as follows: \[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \mathbf{q}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{3} & -30 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{8} \\ 0 & 5 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-4} \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. }^{\Large R} \]

Therefore, \[ r_{11}+r_{13}+r_{23} = 3+8+(-4) = 7. \]

example.title: Finding a QR Factorization of a Matrix Given an Orthogonal Basis in Terms of the Columns of a Matrix

question.text:
\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{q_{11}} & q_{12} \\ q_{21} & q_{22} \\ q_{31} & q_{32} \\ \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} \\ 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{22}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ of $A$ are orthogonal, and that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained by normalizing the columns of $A,$ what is the value of $q_{11} \cdot r_{22}?$
question.explanation:
Since the columns of $A$ are already orthogonal, to construct an orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we simply normalize $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2\mathbf{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf{q}_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{a}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{a}_1 \Vert} =\dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{q}_2 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{a}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{a}_2\Vert} =\dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

\begin{align} R &= Q^T \! A \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{3}{5} & \dfrac{4}{5} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore, we have the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{1} & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 0 & \dfrac{4}{5} \\ \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{5} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R} \]

Finally, $q_{11} \cdot r_{22} = 1 \cdot 5 = 1.$

example.title: Finding a QR Factorization of a Matrix Given a Matrix With Orthogonal Columns

question.text:
\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ 6 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} q_{11} & q_{12} \\ q_{21} & q_{22} \\ q_{31} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{q_{32}} \\ \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} \\ 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{22}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $q_{32} \cdot r_{22}.$
question.explanation:
Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

Step 1. We set $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

Step 2. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

\begin{align} \mathbf{v}_2 &= \mathbf{a}_2- \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{a}_2 \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a}_2-\dfrac{\mathbf{a}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{49}{49} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{q}_1 & = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert} = \dfrac{1}{7} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{q}_2 & =\dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert} = \dfrac{1}{7} \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align}

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} R &= Q^T \! A \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{7} & \dfrac{6}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7} \\ \dfrac{6}{7} & -\dfrac{2}{7} & -\dfrac{3}{7} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ 6 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 7 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ 6 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{7} & \dfrac{6}{7} \\ \dfrac{6}{7} & -\dfrac{2}{7} \\ \dfrac{2}{7} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-\dfrac{3}{7}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 7 \\ 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{7} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Finally, $q_{32} \cdot r_{22} = \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right) \cdot (7) = -3.$

example.title: Finding the QR Factorization of a Matrix

question.text:
\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \mathbf{q}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} &{r_{12}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray] {r_{13}} \\ 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{22}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{23}} \\ 0 & 0 & r_{33} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R} \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{q}_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{a}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_2 + \mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_3 = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{a}_3 +2\mathbf{q}_1 - \mathbf{q}_2 \end{cases} \]

What is the value of $r_{13}+r_{22}+r_{23}?$
question.explanation:
Let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$ \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{q}_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{a}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_2 + \mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_3 = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{a}_3 +2\mathbf{q}_1 - \mathbf{q}_2 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} \mathbf{a}_1 = 4\mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{a}_2 = -2\mathbf{q}_1 + 2\mathbf{q}_2 \\ \mathbf{a}_3 = -6\mathbf{q}_1 +3\mathbf{q}_2 + 3\mathbf{q}_3. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, this system can be written in matrix form as follows: \[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \mathbf{q}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 4 & {-2} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-6} \\ 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{2} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R} \]

Therefore,

\[ r_{13}+r_{22}+r_{23} = -6+ 2 + 3 = -1. \]
